items.name: Bail / release review (Humphrey)
items.authority: In re Humphrey (2021) 11 Cal.5th 135; Pen. Code § 1275
items.purpose: Asks the judge to set release terms the person can actually meet; the court must consider ability to pay and less restrictive conditions.

items.name: Marsden motion (new appointed lawyer)
items.purpose: A private hearing where the client tells the judge why appointed counsel isn't representing them adequately and asks for a different one.

items.name: Discovery request / motion to compel
items.purpose: Makes the prosecution turn over police reports, witness statements and evidence that helps the defense. Informal request first, then a motion after 15 days.

items.name: Brady request (favorable evidence)
items.purpose: The prosecution must disclose evidence favorable to the defense, including anything that undercuts its witnesses.

items.name: Pitchess motion (officer records)
items.authority: Evid. Code §§ 1043, 1045; Pitchess v. Superior Court (1974) 11 Cal.3d 531
items.purpose: Asks the court to review an officer's personnel file for complaints of dishonesty or excessive force that matter to the case.

items.name: Motion to suppress evidence
items.purpose: Asks the court to exclude evidence from an unlawful search or seizure. Can be heard at the preliminary hearing or later in the trial court.

items.name: Timely preliminary hearing
items.purpose: The preliminary hearing must be held within 10 court days of arraignment (in custody) or 60 days (out of custody) unless time is waived.

items.name: Motion to set aside the information (995)
items.purpose: Argues the evidence at the preliminary hearing didn't show probable cause for a charge, or the hearing was unfair. Asks to dismiss that count.

items.name: Reduce a wobbler to a misdemeanor (17(b))
items.purpose: For charges that can be felony or misdemeanor, asks the judge to treat it as a misdemeanor.

items.name: Mental health diversion
items.purpose: Asks to pause the case for treatment; if completed, the charges are dismissed. Eligibility is for the attorney to assess.

items.name: Romero motion (strike a prior)
items.authority: People v. Superior Court (Romero) (1996) 13 Cal.4th 497; Pen. Code § 1385
items.purpose: Asks the judge to dismiss a prior 'strike' conviction in the interest of justice.

items.name: Speedy trial / dismissal for delay
items.purpose: Felony trial within 60 days of arraignment on the information unless time is waived or good cause exists.

items.name: Continuance (or opposing one)
items.purpose: Written motion with 2 court days' notice to move a date; requires good cause.

items.name: Motions in limine
items.purpose: Asks before trial to admit or exclude specific evidence so the jury never hears improper material.

items.name: Motion for acquittal (1118.1)
items.purpose: After the prosecution rests, asks the judge to acquit if the evidence is insufficient.

items.name: Motion for new trial
items.purpose: Asks for a new trial for errors, misconduct or new evidence. Must be made before judgment (sentencing).

items.name: Probation / sentencing statement
items.authority: Pen. Code § 1203; Cal. Rules of Court 4.414, 4.423
items.purpose: Defense statement in mitigation, letters, and objections to the probation report.

items.name: Detention / release-conditions review
items.purpose: Asks the court to revisit detention or change release conditions (travel, GPS, curfew).

items.name: Rule 5(f) Brady order
items.purpose: Court's written order reminding the prosecution of its duty to disclose favorable evidence.

items.name: Preliminary hearing
items.purpose: Within 14 days (in custody) or 21 days (out of custody) of the initial appearance unless indicted first or time is extended.

items.name: Indictment deadline (Speedy Trial Act)
items.purpose: Indictment within 30 days of arrest, or the charge must be dismissed (with or without prejudice) unless time is excluded.

items.name: Discovery (Rule 16) and Brady/Giglio
items.authority: Fed. R. Crim. P. 16; Brady v. Maryland; Giglio v. United States
items.purpose: Requests the defendant's statements, documents, reports, test results, and impeachment material.

items.name: Bill of particulars
items.purpose: Asks the court to make the government spell out the details of a vague charge. Within 14 days after arraignment or later if the court allows.

items.name: Rule 12 motions (dismiss, defects in the indictment)
items.purpose: Must be raised before trial: defects in the indictment, failure to state an offense, improper venue, severance, suppression.

items.name: Motion to suppress evidence
items.authority: Fed. R. Crim. P. 12(b)(3)(C); Fourth Amendment
items.purpose: Asks to exclude evidence from an unlawful search, seizure or interrogation.

items.name: Franks hearing
items.purpose: If an affidavit has knowing or reckless false statements or omissions, asks for a hearing to test it.

items.name: Rule 17(c) subpoena
items.purpose: Court-ordered subpoena for records held by third parties.

items.name: Speedy trial (70 days)
items.purpose: Trial within 70 days of indictment or first appearance, minus excluded time.

items.name: Rule 29 motion for acquittal
items.purpose: Asks the judge to acquit for insufficient evidence; can be renewed within 14 days after the verdict.

items.name: Jury instructions
items.purpose: Defense proposed instructions and objections.

items.name: Rule 33 motion for new trial
items.purpose: Within 14 days of the verdict; within 3 years if based on newly discovered evidence.

items.name: Objections to the presentence report
items.purpose: Written objections within 14 days of receiving the PSR; sentencing memo on the § 3553(a) factors.

if_you_lose.title: Sentencing
if_you_lose.body: The probation department writes a report. The defense can submit a statement in mitigation and character letters, and object to anything wrong in the report.

links.label: Cal. Rules of Court, rule 4.423 (mitigating factors)

if_you_lose.title: Motion for new trial
if_you_lose.body: Asks the trial judge for a new trial because of legal error, misconduct or new evidence. It must be made and decided before judgment is pronounced.

if_you_lose.title: Probation and early termination
if_you_lose.body: If granted probation, the court can end it early once the person has complied and it serves justice.

appeal.title: Notice of appeal — 60 days
appeal.body: A felony notice of appeal must be filed within 60 days after the judgment (sentencing) or the order being appealed. Courts can't extend this deadline. After a guilty or no-contest plea, a certificate of probable cause is usually also needed.

appeal.title: Appointed appellate lawyer
appeal.body: If you can't afford a lawyer, the Court of Appeal appoints one through the appellate project for its district. Orange County is the Fourth District, Division Three (Appellate Defenders, Inc.); Los Angeles is the Second District (California Appellate Project – LA).

links.label: Second District Court of Appeal (Los Angeles) — ask the clerk for the California Appellate Project – LA

appeal.title: Habeas corpus
appeal.body: A habeas petition raises problems outside the trial record, such as ineffective assistance of counsel or new evidence. There's no fixed deadline, but it must be filed without substantial delay.

appeal.title: Record clearing
appeal.body: After probation is completed, a conviction can often be dismissed (expunged). Some records get automatic relief, and arrests that didn't lead to a conviction can be sealed. Felony wobblers can sometimes be reduced to misdemeanors.

appeal.title: Certificate of rehabilitation and pardon
appeal.body: For people who have finished their sentence and stayed out of trouble, a certificate of rehabilitation is a court finding that can lead to a governor's pardon.

if_you_lose.title: Rule 29 and Rule 33 motions
if_you_lose.body: Within 14 days of a guilty verdict, the defense can renew its motion for acquittal (Rule 29) or ask for a new trial (Rule 33). A new-trial motion based on newly discovered evidence can be filed within 3 years.

if_you_lose.title: Sentencing
if_you_lose.body: Probation writes a presentence report (PSR). Objections are due within 14 days of receiving it. The judge must consider the factors in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a), not just the guideline range.

if_you_lose.title: Early termination of supervised release
if_you_lose.body: After one year of supervised release, the court can end it early if conduct and the interest of justice support it.

appeal.title: Notice of appeal — 14 days
appeal.body: In a federal criminal case, the defendant's notice of appeal must be filed in the district court within 14 days after the judgment is entered (or after the government's notice of appeal, if later).

appeal.title: Appointed appellate lawyer (CJA)
appeal.body: A defendant who qualified for appointed counsel keeps that right on appeal. The Ninth Circuit appoints Criminal Justice Act (CJA) counsel.

appeal.title: Motion under 28 U.S.C. § 2255
appeal.body: After the appeal, a § 2255 motion can raise constitutional problems such as ineffective assistance. It generally must be filed within 1 year after the conviction becomes final.

appeal.title: Record clearing and pardon
appeal.body: Federal law has almost no expungement. The main route is a presidential pardon, generally available 5 years after release.

links.label: DOJ Office of the Pardon Attorney

probono.intro: The public defender handles criminal defense for people who can't afford a lawyer. Legal aid groups rarely take criminal cases, but they help with record clearing, re-entry, housing, jobs and benefits. Eligibility is usually income-based.

items.name: Ask the court for a public defender
items.what: If you can't afford a lawyer in a criminal case, you have a right to an appointed one. Ask at your first court date.
items.eligibility: Based on income and assets; the court decides.

items.name: State Bar certified Lawyer Referral Services
items.what: Referral to a screened private lawyer, often with a low-cost first consultation.

items.name: LawHelpCA
items.what: Statewide finder for free legal aid by county and problem type.
items.eligibility: Most programs are for low-income Californians.

items.name: Law school clinics
items.what: Many California law schools run supervised clinics (criminal defense, re-entry, record clearing, innocence projects). Each clinic picks its own cases.
items.eligibility: Varies by clinic; usually low-income, sometimes limited to certain case types.

items.name: Innocence projects (e.g. Northern California Innocence Project)
items.what: Wrongful-conviction cases only, after conviction. Southern California has the California Innocence Project (San Diego) and Loyola's Project for the Innocent.
items.eligibility: Strong claim of actual innocence; long screening process.

premium: The premium (the bail agent's fee) is commonly 10% of the bond amount and must match the rate the surety filed with the Department of Insurance. It's nonrefundable even if the case is dismissed.
Collateral (a car title, property, cash) may be required on top of the premium. It's returned after the bond is exonerated, the case ends, and everything owed is paid.
Payment plans are common. Get the total, the schedule and any fees in writing before you sign.
cosigner: A cosigner (indemnitor) promises to pay the full bond amount if the defendant misses court and isn't brought back. Only cosign for someone you trust to show up.
You can ask the bail agent for copies of everything you sign, the license number of the agent, and a receipt for every payment.
If you're worried the person will miss court, talk to the bail agent right away about your options.
Keep the court dates on your own calendar too, and help with rides.

documents.title: Case packet for the attorney (PDF)
documents.what: Case at a glance, dates and contacts, with the privileged section only if you include it.

documents.title: Character letter template
documents.what: A short guide and template for family, employers and community members. Letters go to the defense attorney, not the court.
documents.body:
To the Honorable Judge of the [Court]:

My name is [name]. I am [relationship] and have known [defendant] for [years].

[Specific examples of character, work, family responsibility, community service.]

I understand the charge in this case. [Optional: what support I will provide — rides to court, housing, job.]

I declare that the above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Sincerely,

documents.title: Authorization: attorney may talk to my family
documents.what: Lets the defense attorney share scheduling and logistics with a named family member. Ask the attorney whether it affects privilege before signing.
documents.body:
I, [client name], authorize my defense attorney, [attorney name], to discuss court dates, logistics, and how my family can help with: [family member name, relationship, phone].

This does not authorize sharing strategy, evidence or privileged communications unless I say so in writing. I may revoke this at any time in writing.

documents.title: Release of records (to my attorney)
documents.what: Authorizes an employer, school, program or doctor to send records to the defense attorney (useful for mitigation).
documents.body:
I, [client name], date of birth [DOB], authorize [organization] to release the following records: [employment / program / school / medical records] to my attorney, [attorney name, address, email].

This authorization expires on [date]. A copy is as valid as the original.

documents.title: Official court forms
documents.what: California Judicial Council forms and local court forms. Waivers and plea forms are given to you by your attorney or the court — don't sign them without your attorney.
